problem: RL-based social navigation methods (e.g., Falcon) need thousands of GPU hours (2,396 h) of training, are reactive, and generalize poorly to new environments without fine-tuning. Prior zero-shot embodied navigation methods cannot handle dynamic human obstacles.
motivation: Robots in crowded indoor spaces must anticipate human motion rather than only react, and deployment requires no environment-specific retraining. The authors observe that simple geometric human trajectory forecasts, inserted as short-lived obstacles into an occupancy map, can give proactive avoidance with a classical planner.
key_idea: Build a depth-based occupancy map, add fused history-based (linear regression) and orientation-based (linear extrapolation) human trajectory predictions as time-decaying dynamic obstacles, and plan with FMM, all training-free.
insight: Dynamic obstacles from predicted human paths mainly cut human collisions (H-Coll 30.36 vs 41.58 for Falcon on Social-HM3D) at the cost of SPL and SR. Ablation on Social-HM3D shows removing dynamic obstacles drops Final Score 61.21 to 56.16, and removing orientation prediction (55.94) hurts more than removing history prediction (59.82). Fusion also matters (57.73 without). The Final Score gain over Falcon is small and comes from the collision term.
method: Static map construction: back-project depth to a 3D point cloud, transform to agent frame, voxelize, and sum over the traversable height range to get a 2D occupancy map (20m x 20m, 5cm/pixel).
Coordinate transformation: convert goal from world to a fixed map frame anchored at the initial agent pose; place an intermediate goal at min(W/3,H/3) toward out-of-bounds goals.
History prediction: least-squares linear regression on the last 10 timesteps of each human's position to extrapolate 10 future steps.
Orientation prediction: extend the human's current heading linearly (0.5 m ahead, step-based) to get future positions.
Trajectory fusion: weighted blend with w_hist = w_base*alpha^k (alpha=0.5) and w_orient = 1 - w_hist, so history dominates near-term and orientation long-term.
Dynamic human obstacles with decay: current and predicted positions are dilated by a 0.25 m disk into the map and cleared after T_decay=5 timesteps.
Path and action: FMM (Eikonal) on the eroded traversability map gives a short-term goal; a deterministic rule picks forward/left/right (15° threshold)/stop.

setting.backbone: none (classical mapping + linear trajectory prediction + Fast Marching Method planner)
setting.observation: egocentric depth + agent pose + observable human positions and orientations
setting.action_space: discrete: move forward, turn left, turn right, stop
setting.privileged: Ground-truth human positions and orientations from the simulator (H_t) and goal position; agent pose

numbers_note: Benchmarks Social-HM3D/Social-MP3D (Falcon's Social-Nav benchmark) are not in the canonical list, so labeled other:. Hyperparameter results are only in a figure. Ablation numbers (Social-HM3D) are in Table 2 but are not repeated as entries.
results: On Social-HM3D the zero-shot method reaches Final Score 61.21 versus Falcon's 60.39, with human collision at 30.36 vs 41.58. On Social-MP3D it gets 56.58 vs 56.19, with H-Coll 30.54 vs 48.53. However SR and SPL are lower than Falcon (51.71/43.91 vs 53.84/49.30; 43.53/37.09 vs 48.47/42.08).
limitations: Lower SR and SPL than Falcon; the Final Score advantage is marginal and depends on the paper's own weighted metric and reproduced Falcon numbers.
Relies on simulator-provided human positions/orientations and linear motion models, which may not hold for real perception noise or nonlinear human behavior; no real-robot tests.
Many hand-set hyperparameters (radius, decay, alpha); the text has an inconsistency (ablation text reports 58.94 for w/o orientation vs 55.94 in the table).
